newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl stays committed to timely euro launch.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl stays committed to timely euro launch.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl remains unalterably committed to Europe's single currency even though he is now stressing that the euro's stability is his top priority, a German government spokesman said on Monday.
Trying to stifle speculation that Kohl's enthusiasm for the proposed single currency was waning, spokesman Herbert Schmuelling insisted Kohl had not had a change of heart.

He rejected the suggestion Kohl was retreating from his long-held stance that the euro should be launched on time in 1999, even though the chancellor made clear in an interview broadcast on Sunday that he was opposed to a weak euro.

"The chancellor said quite clearly that there would be no weak euro," Schmuelling said when asked if Kohl's remarks meant he was now considering a delay in the start of the euro if the stability criteria were not met.
"The schedule and the criteria remain valid as they were in the past," he said. "There has been no change in the mood."

Kohl, in an interview with ZDF television aired on Sunday from his holiday in the Austrian Alps, said monetary stability would not be sacrificed even though he was an ardent supporter of European integration. A weak euro would not be acceptable.
"Whoever believes that Helmut Kohl will give up the policy (of stability) out of enthusiasm for Europe and day-to-day factors... is wrong," Kohl said. "That is a price I will not pay."
Some observers leaped on Kohl's comments as an indication that he was starting to cave in to growing domestic opposition to the highly unpopular currency.

"If the chancellor wants to win the next election in 1998," said German Radio in a commentary, "then he should consider delaying the launch of the euro...the resentment against the proposed death of the Deutschemark will not help his chances."

Countries which want to join monetary union in 1999 must meet targets in inflation and exchange rates, interest rates, deficits and public debt this year. Germany is having problems meeting the deficit goals although growth is now picking up.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt stressed Germany's economy was growing and the country was on track to allow it to qualify for the economic and monetary union.
"We will meet the criteria," Rexrodt said, chanting the Bonn government's mantra on the EMU question.

The Bundesbank, meanwhile, returns from its summer recess this week and economists said the central bank is not expected to make any changes to its credit policies despite heavy speculation in recent weeks that a move was in the pipeline.

Economists disagreed with the view that Kohl was retreating from the single currency, pointing out that the chancellor made repeated references in his 20-minute interview to the fact that the euro would be launched on schedule in 1999.
"Kohl has been emphasising the importance of stability for a long time," said Jens Dallmeyer, an economist at Deutsche Bank's DB Research in Frankfurt.
"But he did not raise any doubts about the time schedule. There is a certain contradiction there. We are nevertheless convinced the euro will be launched on time."

Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, who has whipped up fears about the euro being a weak currency, has said the euro launch should be delayed if countries overshoot the Maastricht budget deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product.

Kohl has already bowed to pressure from Stoiber and pledged to meet the strict 3.0 deficit percent interpretation of the budget deficit criteria, to allay fears of those who believe a fudged currency union would result in a soft euro.

"Kohl's remarks on Sunday need to be seen in view of what Stoiber has been saying, his trying to take advantage of fears in Germany," said Dallmeyer. "But anyone who saw the whole interview would realise there has been no change in Kohl's position."
